description: To create a visual tool that helps astronauts assess their health during space missions and provides them with guidance on treatments and improvements to their well-being.
summary: The ASTRA HEALTH SYSTEM is an autonomous aerospace medical platform developed to monitor astronaut health and support clinical decision-making during spaceflight. Featuring a hybrid two-tiered architecture, the system first processes telemetry through specialized rule engines, statistical models, and temporal trend analyses, then integrates these outputs into a neural network metamodel alongside an interactive questioning module. It addresses long-duration mission risks, such as cephalic fluid shifts, microgravity deconditioning, nephrolithiasis, and orthostatic intolerance, by contextualizing physiological data against pre-flight baselines, flight phases, and NASA risk framework DAGs. Connected via multi-network hardware controllers, it delivers role-tailored operational UI modes for astronauts, medical officers, and systems engineers. Implemented prototype capabilities handle real-time onboard diagnosis, risk stratification, and personalized treatment protocols, while future updates enable periodic off-board neural network retraining on Earth. By enabling autonomous, evidence-based medical oversight, ASTRA safeguards crew health against communication delays, advancing deep-space exploration.
details:
Space Medical Information Processing System (AstraHealth)

To enable the software system to perform monitoring, diagnostic, and treatment functions for astronaut health, its architecture is structured sequentially: first, space environment biomedical phenomena and associated risks are identified; next, relevant clinical indicators are defined; and based on these indicators, measurement devices and technologies are selected to feed data into the software. Because operational conditions vary throughout a mission, these indicators and technologies are tailored to three specific operational scenarios: the intravehicular environment (astronaut without suit), the extravehicular environment (astronaut with suit), and the specialized analysis center onboard the space station for processing complex biological samples.

Following the definition of capture devices, the system addresses information processing through two complementary dimensions: the technical dimension, comprising the software's computational mechanisms, and the clinical dimension, focusing on the diagnostic and therapeutic evaluation flow.

The process is articulated through a two-tiered architecture:

  • Diagnostic Sequence: Tier 01 executes specialized analytical methods (medical rules, statistical models, probabilistic models, and temporal analysis against the astronaut's historical baseline) to encode findings. Subsequently, Tier 02 integrates these inputs using an ensemble neural network metamodel to issue a preliminary evaluation. If the system detects critical uncertainty or data gaps, it triggers an interactive questioning module that feeds back into the analysis before confirming the final diagnosis.
  • Treatment Sequence: Upon diagnostic confirmation, Tier 01 deploys applicable therapeutic options and protocols. These options are then filtered considering the astronaut's biological profile, active complications, and available onboard medical resources. Finally, Tier 02 (the PTRS neural network for personalized treatment recommendation) evaluates the optimal alternative to generate an interactive action plan with real-time continuous monitoring.

With the processing algorithms established, the hardware infrastructure and network topology organize the telemetric flow according to the operational environment:

  • Intravehicular Environment (IVA): Wearable devices connect via a Wireless Body Network (WBN) to a Body Controller, which transmits telemetry over the local network to the central station computer for historical logging and relay to Earth.
  • Extravehicular Environment (EVA): Suit-integrated sensors transmit data over a dedicated Suit Network to the Suit Controller—housed in the suit backpack with local storage capacity for up to one month—which communicates with the station computer via a signal-intermittent-tolerant network protocol.
  • Analysis Center: Advanced diagnostic equipment links through the Analysis Center Network to its dedicated Analysis Center Controller, which centralizes advanced testing and synchronizes records with the station computer.

To implement this ecosystem during crewed missions, the final interface prototype and its interactive web simulation were developed (available at https://www.astrahealth.earth/). Designed under the principle of information simplification to prevent cognitive overload in crew members, the platform manages data using an automatic time-in-flight switch that detects the current flight phase (microgravity entry, in-flight adaptation, and return) and adjusts evaluation parameters to match the astronaut's physiological variations, thereby preventing false positives in diagnosis and treatment.

The interface segments information into three operational modes tailored to the user's role:

  1. Astronaut Mode: Prioritizes rapid self-management through color-coded anatomical mapping, countermeasure tracking, and live interactive questioning.
  2. Medical Mode: Focused on deep clinical evaluation, neurophysiological sleep tracking, and longitudinal physiological trend analysis.
  3. Systems Mode: Dedicated to technical hardware diagnostics and continuous monitoring of intra- and extravehicular network infrastructure.

Finally, the visual presentation modality adapts dynamically to crew equipment: in intravehicular activities (without suit), information is displayed via holographic projection on contact lenses or through a monitor screen on the station if contact lenses are omitted; in extravehicular activities (with suit), visualization occurs via holographic projection on the helmet visor, while maintaining operational control exclusively through voice commands across all scenarios.
